title: Short Stuff: "Peace" Pipes
summary: Short Stuff episode explaining that "peace pipes" is a misnomer: Native American sacred or ceremonial pipes (calumets) were used widely across North America for prayer, solemn occasions, treaties, weddings and other ceremonies, not only for peace treaties. Covers the pipe's separate pieces (stem, bowl, mouthpiece) that are kept apart until a ceremony begins, the use of pipestone (including red pipestone from Pipestone National Monument in Minnesota and its permit and digging restrictions), other materials, sacred smoking plants such as kinnikinnick and traditional tobacco (not marijuana), and the Lakota white buffalo calf woman origin story. The hosts close by noting the practice is still living culture, citing an interview with Gabriel Drapeau of the Yankton Sioux tribe.

segments.title: Peace pipes misnomer
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the topic and explain that 'peace pipes' is the wrong term; these are sacred or ceremonial pipes used across North America, not only for treaties.

segments.title: Widespread use and calumet name
segments.summary: Ceremonial pipes are found across North America from Florida to the Midwest, the Hopewell culture in Ohio, and the Southwest to the Pacific Northwest. The broader term is calumet, and pipes were used for prayer, treaties, parties and other occasions.

segments.title: Meanings and parts of the pipe
segments.summary: Meanings vary by tribe; smoke carries prayers to the spirit world. The Lakota origin story involves White Buffalo Calf Woman. Pipes come in separate pieces that are kept apart and joined to begin a ceremony.

segments.title: Brief transition
segments.summary: Light banter and a pun about pieces versus peace, then a segment transition.

segments.title: Pipestone and red pipestone
segments.summary: Pipes are often made of pipestone, with red pipestone from Pipestone National Monument in southwest Minnesota considered especially sacred. Catlinite is clay-based and easy to work, but access requires a permit limited to enrolled tribal members, hand tools, and digging beneath quartz, often taking multiple visits.

segments.title: Other materials, stems and sacred smoke
segments.summary: Pipes can also be made of limestone, bone, pottery or shale. Stems are often wood and may be decorated with feathers and beadwork. Smoking materials include kinnikinnick (bearberry) and traditional tobacco, not marijuana, which the hosts call a myth from non-Native jokes.

segments.title: Ceremonial use and treaty sealing
segments.summary: Pipes are assembled from separate parts for ceremonies such as sweat lodges and weddings. In some cultures they sealed peace treaties between warring nations: a medicine man joins the pipe pieces brought by two chiefs.

segments.title: Living tradition
segments.summary: Hosts note that the practice continues today, citing an interview with Gabriel Drapeau of the Yankton Sioux tribe who says the culture is not in the past tense.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the short episode and the show's production credit is read.
